hypotheses.reasoning: Trigger: redis was replaced and restarted at 19:58:49 with no RDB snapshot, so it came back with 0 keys (#1023). Order-service's cache hit rate collapsed: miss ratio hit 96% against a 2% baseline and it fell back to postgres for every read (#1089). Every miss became a SELECT on orders, and those queries slowed to 5-9s (#1090, #1428). Postgres then ran out of headroom: connections 490/500 with CPU at 96% (#1107, #1159). Order-service queries timed out after 5s (#1236), and the gateway returned 504s after 13-24s (#1173). The trigger was a single cache restart, and the outage came from every cache miss hitting the database, so this is amplification rather than a DB fault. Confidence is 0.8 rather than higher because the postgres connection exhaustion is also a plausible reading of the same lines. Ruled out: the status-poller timeouts to legacy-inventory (#712, #1164 and others) are a deprecated healthcheck endpoint and do not touch the checkout path; the vacuum and checkpoint lines show nothing unusual.

Alternative reading: postgres connection slots (500) and CPU were exhausted under the post-restart load, so the pool limit is the binding constraint. This explains the timeouts, but the trigger is the cache loss, which makes it a downstream effect of the cascade rather than the origin.

verdict.recommendedAction: Restore redis cache capacity: re-warm the cache or bring up a replica that has data from before the node swap. In the short term, shed or rate-limit checkout, or raise the postgres connection limit and add a cache-stampede guard so misses do not all query postgres. Persist redis snapshots (RDB/AOF) so a node replacement does not start empty. Separately, remove the deprecated legacy-inventory healthcheck from status-poller.

Order-service's cache hit rate collapsed: miss ratio hit 96% against a 2% baseline and it fell back to postgres for every read (#1089).
